items.title: FG destroys 1,419 illicit weapons, recovers 5,449 firearms in 2026
items.description: The National Centre for the Control of Small Arms and Light Weapons (NCCSALW) has destroyed 1,419 illicit weapons and recovered 5,449 firearms in recent operations nationwide. The ​‌‍‍‍‍⁠⁠‌‍​⁠‍​‍⁠‍‌​director-general of the centre, retired DIG Johnson Kokumo, made this known on Tuesday in Abuja at the Joint Security News Briefing. The briefing was organised for spokespersons of defence, security and law-enforcement agencies to update Nigerians on ongoing security efforts. Kokumo said the 1,419 weapons were publicly destroyed on July 30 during the centre’s second quarter arms destruction exercise in Abuja. He said the exercise brought the total number of illicit weapons destroyed by NCCSALW since 2022 to more than 19,000. According to him, the destruction is aimed at preventing illicit weapons from reaching non-state actors and fuelling terrorism, banditry, kidnapping and other violent crimes. Kokumo said the Centre also recorded significant recoveries through collaboration with security and law-enforcement agencies. He said 5,050 illicit, unserviceable, decommissioned and obsolete automatic weapons were retrieved from the Nigeria Police Force in June. He added that the Nigeria Customs Service intercepted and handed over 399 JOJEF automatic guns to NCCSALW on Aug. 17. The director-general said other weapons had also been recovered from the National Drug Law Enforcement Agency and the National Intelligence Agency. He said the centre was collaborating with relevant justice-sector institutions to prosecute persons involved in arms trafficking, illegal importation and manufacture. Kokumo said 11 suspects linked to the illegal importation of 844 assorted automatic firearms and 112,500 rounds of ammunition were arrested. The weapons and ammunition were concealed in a container intercepted by the Nigeria Customs Service at Onne Port and handed over to NCCSALW. He said the principal suspects remained in custody, while investigations continued to apprehend other fleeing suspects. Kokumo also disclosed the arrest and prosecution of suspects linked to the illegal manufacture of firearms and ammunition in Minna, Niger State. On weapons management, he said the centre conducted physical security and stockpile management training for personnel of arms-bearing security agencies. The training, conducted from May 18 to June 19, was designed to prevent the diversion of legally held weapons into criminal circulation. Kokumo said NCCSALW also commenced steps towards a new national small arms survey to replace the 2016 survey, which no longer reflected current realities. He said the centre held a baseline workshop on Aug. 20 with representatives of UN agencies, Small Arms Survey, security agencies and relevant government institutions. According to him, the new survey will provide updated data to guide national responses to the proliferation of illicit small arms and light weapons. Kokumo further urged Nigerians to distinguish the federal government’s National Forest Guards initiative from the illegal Nigeria Forest Security Service. He said the National Forest Guards initiative was coordinated by the Office of the National Security Adviser. The director-general said key members of the illegal group, including its leader, Joshua Osatimehin, had been arrested and were facing prosecution. He added that a court order had also directed the sealing of the group’s offices nationwide. Kokumo reaffirmed NCCSALW’s commitment to working with security agencies, international partners and other stakeholders to reduce the circulation of illicit weapons. He called for continued public cooperation and accurate information sharing to support efforts to deny criminal elements access to arms. He said the destruction of seized illicit weapons was in line with international conventions on arms control, adding that Nigeria was a signatory to them. ( NAN ) The post FG destroys 1,419 illicit weapons, recovers 5,449 firearms in 2026 appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Travellers can take up to GH¢500 in Ghanaian currency out of the country – Customs
items.description: The Ghana Revenue Authority’s (GRA) Customs Division has reminded passengers travelling outside Ghana that they are permitted to carry a maximum of GH¢500 in Ghanaian currency. Revenue Officer at the Accra International Airport Preventive Unit, Conrad Attu, said passengers who exceed the limit risk having the excess amount seized at the point of departure. Speaking on Joy FM’s Super Morning Show on Tuesday, September 1, Mr Attu said: “When travelling outside, outbound passengers are only allowed to carry 500 cedis on them. Beyond that, they might be seized.” He explained that the restriction is based on the expectation that travellers would use the currency of their destination rather than carry large amounts of Ghanaian currency abroad. “We assume that in the other country, you might not need to have any Ghana cedis. You use the currency of that particular country,” he said. The clarification forms part of broader guidance from Customs on the rules governing the movement of cash and other items across Ghana’s borders. Customs has also urged travellers to familiarise themselves with currency declaration requirements before arriving at the airport to avoid complications during the departure process. Passengers can visit the Customs office at the airport to make the necessary declarations regarding the currency they are carrying. Mr Attu stressed that passengers carrying significant amounts of cash should complete all relevant procedures before checking in their luggage. The GH¢500 limit applies specifically to Ghanaian currency being taken out of the country. Foreign currencies are subject to separate declaration requirements. Customs therefore advises passengers travelling abroad to plan their currency needs carefully and seek clarification from its officers at the airport if they are uncertain about the applicable requirements.

items.title: US lists two family visa options for foreigners seeking permanent residence
items.description: The United States Government has outlined two family-based immigrant visa categories available to foreign nationals seeking to move to the country permanently through qualifying family relationships. The US Department of State said foreign citizens seeking permanent residence in the country through family connections must obtain an immigrant visa and meet the requirements for their respective category. According to the department, there are two main types of family-based immigrant visas: Immediate Relative and Family Preference. The Immediate Relative category is available to people with close family relationships to US citizens. It covers spouses, unmarried children under 21 and parents of US citizens who are at least 21 years old. One major advantage of the Immediate Relative category is that there is no annual numerical limit on the number of immigrants who can be admitted through it. The second category is the Family Preference visa, which covers certain more distant family relationships with US citizens as well as specified relationships with lawful permanent residents, commonly known as green-card holders. Unlike Immediate Relative visas, Family Preference visas are subject to annual numerical limits. This means applicants in these categories may have to wait until an immigrant visa becomes available. The US government said the Family Preference category includes unmarried sons and daughters aged 21 or older of US citizens, spouses and unmarried children of lawful permanent residents, married sons and daughters of US citizens, and brothers and sisters of adult US citizens. The State Department’s September 2026 Visa Bulletin shows that family-sponsored preference visas remain subject to numerical limits and priority dates, with availability determined according to the relevant category and applicant’s country of chargeability. For Nigerians and other foreigners hoping to relocate to the United States through family sponsorship, the distinction between the two categories is important. Those who qualify as immediate relatives of US citizens are not subject to the annual numerical cap applicable to family-preference categories. However, applicants under the preference categories may face waiting periods before a visa becomes available. The US Citizenship and Immigration Services also states that US citizens and lawful permanent residents can generally petition for eligible relatives by filing Form I-130, Petition for Alien Relative. The US Department of State’s official family immigration guidance is the source for the two-category classification and the rules concerning numerical limits. The post US lists two family visa options for foreigners seeking permanent residence appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Mahama renews Ghana’s call for end to US economic embargo on Cuba
items.description: President John Mahama has reiterated Ghana’s call for an end to the long-standing economic, commercial, and financial embargo against Cuba, arguing that unilateral measures against sovereign states undermine the principles of the international system. Addressing the 65th anniversary meeting of the Non-Aligned Movement in Belgrade, President Mahama said Ghana remained opposed to the embargo and urged a reconsideration of measures that, in his view, weaken sovereign equality and non-interference. “Ghana reiterates its call to the long-standing economic, commercial, and financial embargo against Cuba,” he said. President Mahama criticised what he described as unilateral coercive measures that undermine the principles of the United Nations Charter. “Unilateral, coercive measures that undermine sovereign equality, non-interference, and purposes and principles of the Charter weaken the multilateral system we all agreed to defend,” he stated. He said the issue of Cuba was part of Ghana’s position that political independence must be matched by the economic capacity of countries to determine their own development priorities. “Political independence is more meaningful when it is accompanied by the economic capacity to pursue national priorities,” President Mahama said. He also called for greater attention to resource sovereignty, arguing that countries in the Global South should not remain trapped in a system where they export raw materials while importing finished products and bearing the environmental and social costs of extraction. President Mahama further urged the Non-Aligned Movement to strengthen its collective voice on global challenges, including climate change, development, finance, and international inequality. “We must speak with one united voice to advance advocacy and action on climate change,” he said. He stressed that the movement must translate its principles into concrete action, particularly as developing countries confront widening development gaps and emerging challenges such as artificial intelligence and digital inequality. “Ghana remains committed to working with all members of the Non-Aligned Movement to strengthen multilateralism, advance a fairer international order and ensure the voice of the Global South carries greater weight,” President Mahama said. The U.S. economic embargo on Cuba dates back to 1960, following the deterioration of relations after Fidel Castro’s revolution and the Cuban government’s nationalisation of U.S.-owned property. President John F. Kennedy formally expanded the trade embargo in February 1962, as Washington sought to put economic pressure on the Cuban government. The restrictions were later reinforced through legislation, including the Cuban Democracy Act of 1992 and the Helms-Burton Act of 1996. While U.S.-Cuba diplomatic relations were restored in 2015 under President Barack Obama and some restrictions were eased, the wider economic embargo remains in force.

items.title: Drive to Inspire – Africa challenges UESD students to build resilient, sustainable futures
items.description: Students at the University of Environment and Sustainable Development (UESD) in Somanya, Eastern Region, have been encouraged to take an active role in shaping their careers, strengthening their mental well-being, and contributing to sustainable development. The call was made during an outreach organised by Drive to Inspire – Africa, which brought together students for conversations around career development, mental health, financial growth, and sustainable development. Speaking on career development, Neil Oku, Founder and C.E.O. of Golden Coast Developers, encouraged students to stay informed about local and international developments and to set clear goals for their personal and professional growth. Attendees were advised to start with small, achievable steps and gradually scale their efforts as they gain experience and develop. He also challenged students to look beyond competing with existing brands and instead pay attention to problems within their communities that could inspire innovative solutions. Such solutions, Mr. Oku noted, could potentially be developed into businesses while also addressing real community needs. The conversation also turned to mental health and the role of mindset in personal development. Dr. Masha Bashiru, a senior clinical and health psychologist, explained that mindset influences how individuals think, perceive themselves, and understand the environment around them. Students were introduced to the concepts of fixed and growth mindsets. While a fixed mindset can make an individual resistant to change, a growth mindset encourages people to embrace progressive changes and continuously improve themselves. Dr. Masha also highlighted the tendency for people to conceal their true mental state behind routine greetings and interactions. She explained the importance of creating environments where young people can openly discuss their mental well-being. Financial literacy formed another key part of the outreach, with Elvis Dan-Sekyi, Head of Distribution and Channels for United Bank for Africa Ghana Limited (UBA), engaging students on developing healthy money habits. Under the theme “Money Moves, Secure Your Future,” the session emphasised that financial success is not determined solely by how much money a person earns, but also by how effectively they manage it. Students were introduced to the principle of “pay yourself first,” which encourages individuals to set aside a portion of their income for saving and investing before spending what remains. The session also encouraged attendees to start small when building a savings habit, with emphasis on consistency rather than the amount saved. Additionally, sustainability professional Christian Adjei Dompreh engaged students on sustainable development and encouraged them to see themselves as active contributors to the development of their communities and Ghana as a whole. He introduced students to the three pillars of sustainable development and highlighted issues including resource management, climate change, inclusion, natural resource governance, renewable energy and the growing opportunities presented by green jobs. This outreach forms part of Drive to Inspire – Africa’s commitment to equipping young people with the knowledge, perspectives, and opportunities needed to reach their potential and become meaningful contributors to their communities and beyond.

items.title: Mahama challenges Non-Aligned Movement to move from declarations to action
items.description: President John Dramani Mahama has challenged the Non-Aligned Movement (NAM) to move beyond declarations and translate its commitments into coordinated action capable of producing practical outcomes in addressing global challenges. He said the movement’s strength should not be measured only by its numbers but by its ability to use its collective influence to achieve meaningful results through coordinated diplomacy. President Mahama made the call at a high-level commemorative meeting marking the 65th anniversary of the First Conference of Heads of State or Government of Non-Aligned Countries in Belgrade, Serbia. He said the principles that informed the establishment of the Movement remained relevant 65 years after its first conference, particularly at a time of growing global tensions and uncertainty. “We must move from declarations to actions,” President Mahama said. He recalled the position taken by former Yugoslav President Josip Broz Tito at the first conference of the Heads of State and Government of the Non-Aligned Movement in Belgrade on September 1, 1961. According to President Mahama, President Tito said non-aligned countries could no longer reconcile themselves with the status of observers and voters and had the right to participate in resolving problems, particularly those that endangered global peace and the fate of the world. “Here we are 65 years later,” President Mahama said. He said the assertion made at the founding conference remained relevant and should inform how the movement operates and responds to global challenges. “This profound assertion remains very relevant. The movement’s strength should be measured not only by our numbers but also by our ability to translate its collective weight into coordinated diplomacy and practical outcomes,” he said. Stronger coordination President Mahama called for stronger consultation and coordination among NAM member states, particularly within the United Nations and other multilateral institutions where their interests converge. He said greater coordination would enable member states to use their collective influence more effectively in international affairs. “We must strengthen consultation and coordination among member states, particularly within the United Nations and other multilateral institutions where our interests converge,” he said. The president also called for stronger follow-up to decisions taken at NAM summits and ministerial conferences. He urged member states to identify and focus on strategic priorities where the Movement could make a meaningful impact, rather than allowing declarations and decisions to remain without corresponding action. “We should therefore strengthen follow-up decisions of our summits and ministerial conferences and focus on strategic priorities where the movement can have meaningful impact,” he said. Serbia pledges stronger partnerships The president of the host country, Serbia, Aleksandar Vučić, assured members of the Non-Aligned Movement that his country was seeking to build stronger partnerships with NAM countries. He said Serbia was looking to create opportunities for more students from NAM countries to travel to Serbia to pursue their education. The commemorative meeting in Belgrade marks 65 years since the first Conference of Heads of State or Government of Non-Aligned Countries was held in the Serbian capital.

items.title: Sitanium Cissé parle aussi de « Lilou » Kaba : un mathématicien amoureux du football à la conquête de la FEGUIFOOT
items.description: Et si les mathématiques pouvaient aussi servir à remettre de l’ordre dans le football guinéen ? Docteur en mathématiques appliquées, ancien universitaire et ancien haut responsable de l’État, Ibrahima Kalil Kaba, affectueusement appelé « Lilou », semble aujourd’hui vouloir mettre son expérience, sa rigueur et son sens de la gestion au service d’un autre univers qui lui est cher : le football. La candidature de Lilou à la présidence de la Fédération guinéenne de football intervient dans un contexte où le football guinéen aspire plus que jamais à retrouver la stabilité, la crédibilité et la performance. L’Assemblée générale élective de la FEGUIFOOT est annoncée pour le **27 octobre 2026 à Conakry. Des mathématiques au football : une même exigence, celle de la rigueur On pourrait se demander ce qu’un mathématicien vient chercher à la tête d’une fédération de football. La réponse est peut-être justement dans les mathématiques : analyser, planifier, anticiper, résoudre les problèmes et prendre des décisions sur la base de données et d’objectifs précis. Lilou Kaba possède un doctorat en mathématiques appliquées obtenu aux États-Unis et a enseigné à Louisiana Tech University. Son parcours l’a ensuite conduit vers les hautes responsabilités administratives et politiques. Mais derrière le scientifique et l’ancien homme d’État se trouve également un passionné du football. Son engagement dans la gestion de Karifamoriah FC lui a permis de se rapprocher davantage du terrain et des réalités quotidiennes du football guinéen. Le club a d’ailleurs atteint la finale de la West Africa Champions Cup. Un dirigeant qui veut fédérer L’un des principaux arguments avancés autour de sa candidature est sa capacité à rassembler. Ces dernières années, la gouvernance du football guinéen a été marquée par des tensions et des crises institutionnelles. Des observateurs estiment ainsi que le profil de Lilou pourrait contribuer à tourner la page des divisions et à instaurer davantage de sérénité dans la gestion de la FEGUIFOOT. Son projet semble également bénéficier de soutiens importants dans le milieu sportif. L’AS Kaloum a officiellement annoncé son parrainage et son soutien à sa candidature, mettant notamment en avant son expérience, sa crédibilité et sa capacité à fédérer. Le football ne se joue pas seulement avec les pieds Aujourd’hui, le football moderne est devenu une véritable industrie : infrastructures, formation, finances, marketing, gouvernance, statistiques, compétitions internationales et développement du football à la base. Dans cet environnement complexe, un profil habitué à l’analyse, à la planification et à la gestion des systèmes complexes peut constituer un atout. Lilou Kaba devra toutefois démontrer que son expérience académique, administrative et sportive peut se transformer en résultats concrets pour le football guinéen : un championnat plus compétitif, des clubs mieux structurés, une meilleure formation des jeunes, des infrastructures adaptées et surtout une équipe nationale capable de rivaliser durablement avec les meilleures nations africaines. Le choix d’un nouveau départ ? La bataille pour la présidence de la FEGUIFOOT s’annonce ouverte, avec plusieurs candidatures qui se dessinent déjà. Lilou Kaba a désormais choisi de s’engager dans cette compétition. Le mathématicien amoureux du football entre donc dans l’arène. Reste maintenant une équation à résoudre : comment transformer la passion en projet, le projet en organisation et l’organisation en résultats ? Le 27 octobre prochain, les électeurs de la FEGUIFOOT auront la responsabilité de choisir celui qui devra conduire le football guinéen vers une nouvelle étape. Et pour Lilou Kaba, l’équation est désormais posée. À lui de démontrer que, dans le football comme dans les mathématiques, une bonne méthode peut conduire à de grands résultats. Mohamed Sita Cissé – “Sitanium” L’article Sitanium Cissé parle aussi de « Lilou » Kaba : un mathématicien amoureux du football à la conquête de la FEGUIFOOT est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .

items.title: Permit from Interior Ministry required to import arms, ammunition – GRA
items.description: The Ghana Revenue Authority (GRA) has cautioned travellers that arms and ammunition cannot be imported into Ghana as ordinary personal effects and require prior approval from the Ministry of the Interior. According to a Revenue Officer at the Accra International Airport Preventive Unit, Conrad Attu, firearms and ammunition are subject to strict regulatory controls because of their restricted nature. Speaking on Joy FM’s Super Morning Show on Tuesday, September 1, Mr Attu said anyone seeking to import arms or ammunition must obtain the necessary permit from the Ministry of the Interior before bringing the items into the country. “Before any person would import any arm or ammunition, you will have to get a permit from the Ministry of Interior prior to importation,” he said. He explained that Customs officers would examine the items upon arrival and verify whether the importer had the required permit. “We would also make sure we conduct the examination and confirm if you have the necessary permit,” he added. Mr Attu said even where the appropriate permit had been obtained, the items could be detained at the airport pending further processing by the Ministry of the Interior. The GRA therefore urged travellers to secure all necessary approvals before attempting to bring firearms or ammunition into Ghana to avoid delays or other complications at the airport.

items.title: GIIF records GH¢1.62bn loss in 2025 after GH¢2bn profit in 2024
items.description: The Ghana Infrastructure Investment Fund (GIIF) recorded a net loss of GH¢1.62 billion in 2025, reversing the GH¢2 billion profit achieved in the previous year. According to the 2025 State Ownership Report by the State Interests and Governance Authority (SIGA), the reversal followed a sharp decline in income, rising operating costs and a GH¢1.87 billion foreign-exchange loss. The Fund’s performance deteriorated by approximately GH¢3.62 billion between 2024 and 2025. GIIF had recorded profits of GH¢232.66 million in 2021, GH¢895.77 million in 2022, GH¢497.60 million in 2023 and GH¢2 billion in 2024 before slipping into a loss in 2025. Its net profit margin consequently plunged from 96.76 per cent in 2024 to negative 119.16 per cent in 2025, while return on equity fell from 31.68 per cent to negative 33.39 per cent. The report attributed the loss largely to the movement of the Ghana cedi, which turned a substantial exchange gain in 2024 into a significant loss in 2025. “GIIF further made an exchange loss of GH¢1,868.16 million in FY2025, whereas it made an exchange gain of GH¢1,253.52 million in FY2024 arising from the appreciation of the Ghana cedi during the period,” SIGA said. The Fund’s total income also declined by 37.86 per cent, from GH¢813.33 million in 2024 to GH¢505.39 million in 2025. SIGA said the decline was partly driven by a 22.47 per cent shortfall in interest income, which fell from GH¢605.78 million to GH¢469.64 million. Operating profit decreased by about 58 per cent, from GH¢768.26 million in 2024 to GH¢324.41 million in 2025. GIIF’s net operating margin also dropped from 94.46 per cent to 64.19 per cent, while its cost-recovery ratio declined sharply from 626.59 per cent to 193.46 per cent. The Fund simultaneously experienced a steep rise in operating costs during the year. “The operating cost in the year increased by 290.25 per cent, mainly because of a 301.57 per cent increase in general and administration expenses from GH¢45.07 million to GH¢180.99 million,” the report stated. GIIF’s balance sheet also contracted, with total assets falling from GH¢7.83 billion in 2024 to GH¢5.83 billion in 2025, representing a decline of about 25.5 per cent. Earning assets decreased from GH¢6.01 billion to GH¢4.43 billion, while investment securities fell from GH¢1.62 billion to GH¢1.33 billion. Cash and cash equivalents declined by about 22 per cent, from GH¢1.77 billion in 2024 to GH¢1.38 billion in 2025. Shareholders’ equity also dropped from GH¢6.31 billion to GH¢4.86 billion as the year’s loss reduced the Fund’s accumulated financial resources. “The Fund’s equity followed a similar trend, losing 29.79 per cent to close the year at GH¢4,864 million, occasioned by about GH¢1,624.31 million loss in the period,” SIGA stated. GIIF’s equity multiplier increased from 1.10 times in 2024 to 1.24 times in 2025, indicating a marginal rise in the use of liabilities relative to equity. SIGA, however, assessed the level of leverage as remaining within an acceptable risk threshold. Total liabilities declined from GH¢1.52 billion in 2024 to GH¢968.55 million in 2025. The Fund reported external loans of GH¢961.06 million, accounts payable of GH¢6.02 million and lease liabilities of GH¢1.46 million. Although the Fund’s liquid assets-to-total assets ratio declined from 78.6 per cent to 76.9 per cent, its liquid assets remained more than sufficient to cover its current liabilities. Net cash generated from operating activities also improved sharply from a negative GH¢28.14 million in 2024 to GH¢1.72 billion in 2025. GIIF was established to mobilise and manage financial resources for investment in infrastructure projects across sectors including energy, transport, mining, agribusiness, information and communications technology, hospitality and affordable housing.

items.title: The Growing Lawlessness in California’s Forests
items.description: O n the day of the kidnapping , the campground at Gumboot Lake happened to be nearly empty, so Joseph Charles Henrichsen was one of the only people to see the two Forest Service biologists pull up in their pickup truck. Federal employees didn’t visit all that much—campers who’d been coming to the small alpine lake for years told me they’d never seen a ranger on patrol in these Northern California woods. But some of the regulars had noticed the “frog people,” as one called them, quietly collecting their specimens the previous summer. These particular biologists, both women, were there to survey the Cascades frog, whose well-being can help signal the health of the overall ecosystem. People at Gumboot Lake tended to give one another space, but that July morning, Henrichsen approached the biologists as they worked. He was holding, authorities would later allege, an AR-15-style assault rifle, and told the biologists to turn around and put their hands in the air. He zip-tied their wrists behind their backs and ordered them to walk to his camping trailer, parked at a site strewn with crates and refuse, the clothesline heavy with towels. His 23-year-old son, Phoenix, made room for the biologists inside. What Henrichsen’s intention was that day—what he thought he might achieve by abducting two government scientists, whether he had a clear motivation at all beyond an impulse of self-righteousness and a loaded gun—remains uncertain. Before long, he escorted one of the biologists back to their Forest Service truck. He drove several miles with her down a winding road along the Sacramento River. Glimpses of Mount Shasta, the volcano looming to the east, reared up through the trees. Along the way, he made calls, according to the FBI. He spoke with a Forest Service ranger and left a message with another person who has not been identified. “I’ve taken two Fed biologists hostage from the Forest Service,” he said, according to authorities. “What I’d like to have happen, I’d like to have you send me a fucking Fed investigator, with a goddamn badge, preferably from the FBI. And we can talk things through a little bit.” Over the next few hours, Gumboot Lake and the surrounding Shasta-Trinity National Forest would swarm with law enforcement in helicopters and Bearcat armored vehicles. Local SWAT teams and snipers, then more than 50 FBI officers, poured into the national forest. A Boeing 757 flew across the country, from Virginia, with an elite FBI hostage-rescue team. All of these officers were confronting a man who had a history of erratic behavior: Henrichsen had been released from a Washington State psychiatric hospital a few years before, after allegedly tormenting a neighbor by firing a gun, throwing fireworks on his porch, and placing zip-tie handcuffs on his property. But Henrichsen had also managed to stay at Gumboot Lake for months—well past the official seven-day limit—apparently without triggering any official response from the Forest Service. Many of the campsite’s regulars had crossed paths with the Henrichsens over the summer, and although Charles held himself apart, he struck them as a familiar type, not so out of place here among the free spirits and drifters living in their cars. That he’d turned out to be unhinged or anti-government enough to kidnap a couple of federal frog biologists didn’t seem to shock them. In fact, with the way things are going on the woollier fringes of America’s public lands, maybe something like this was bound to happen. S iskiyou County , the area that includes Gumboot Lake, has a reputation for fierce independence and the hostility toward government meddling that often comes with it. The county leans conservative, though Mount Shasta is a magnet for a crunchier type: crystal enthusiasts, New Age spiritualists, pilgrims on the road to Burning Man. Hikers stream down the Pacific Crest Trail, which runs along a ridge above the lake. On Sundays, some of the campers at Gumboot Lake like to gather for a drum circle, and when the full moon arrives, people convene to celebrate. The Gumboot Lake campground is free and has no assigned spots, no running water, limited cell signal, and a lone pit toilet. It’s one of dozens of alpine lakes in the Trinity Divide accessible by car or off-road vehicle. Others are more popular. The Forest Service described the campground in one write-up as a “typical meadow type lake, not very beautiful.” But it’s relatively easy to get to, just a 40-minute drive up from Interstate 5. I made that drive last month, not long after the Forest Service had reopened Gumboot Lake, less than a week after the kidnapping. I saw old vans and school buses parked along the Forest Service road leading to the campsite; people had strung up hammocks between the trees. At the lake, several campers had already set up their tents and parked their mobile homes. One camper, a 24-year-old backpacker from Australia, told me the campsite was a place to “drop in with the land, drop in with each other, cook meals with each other, and just be super present.” As we talked, a large shirtless man, whom she called Zephyr, appeared and handed her a slice of papaya. The Forest Service is supposed to be a steward of its public lands, preserving them while still allowing people to enjoy the woods and use their resources. Dispersed camping—outside of established campgrounds—is allowed in most national forests. And although people here are supposed to move on after seven nights, locals say that plenty of people live out of their cars for much longer. Informal settlements are widespread on the national-forest lands of Oregon and Northern California. People tend to cluster along the river corridors, most of them peaceable campers. “But the last 10 percent of them are pretty sad,” says Gabriel Howe, the executive director of the Siskiyou Mountain Club, a group that maintains trails and campgrounds in the region. “People living out there, people manufacturing drugs and all sorts of nasty stuff.” Policing a remote forest is unlike any other job in law enforcement. The Shasta-Trinity spans more than 3,000 square miles, and the Forest Service is perennially under-resourced. Carmen Kinch, a Forest Service law officer who patrolled the area around Gumboot Lake in the late 1990s and 2000s, told me that back then, seven law-enforcement officers worked across the entire forest. Today, there are four. Not one, she said, is currently based in the Forest Service management unit that includes Gumboot Lake. The drop in personnel is not just a problem in this one forest. Since last year, the Forest Service’s staffing across the country has fallen by about 20 percent as a result of firings and departures encouraged by the Trump administration, part of its push to reduce the federal workforce. In the Shasta-Trinity forest, excluding firefighting roles, the permanent staff—employees who maintain campsites and conduct wildlife research—has been reduced by about a quarter, one former U.S. official, speaking on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the topic, told me. (Bob Doucette, a Forest Service spokesperson, told me that staffing levels are “similar” to what they’ve been in the past few years and said that “all employees continue to meet public needs.”) Howe has worked in the region for 15 years, and he sees the Forest Service as a slowly dying patient. “Around COVID, it went into palliative care, and now it’s on hospice,” he told me. A sense of lawlessness seems to be growing on the public lands in the region. People on Howe’s staff have returned to find their cars stripped at trailheads—no wheels, no batteries, gas siphoned. They’ve encountered mountain roads blockaded by hostile civilians. Michael Kauffmann, an ecologist and the executive director of the Bigfoot Trail Alliance, told me that he’s recently instituted more training for his researchers and trail crews on safety measures and defusing confrontations. More than anything, Kauffmann has noticed a greater disregard for the rules—more graffiti, a lot more garbage, and less appreciation for these lands as places to care for rather than to joyride over with guns and four-wheelers. One person who regularly hikes in the area around Gumboot Lake told me that he’d felt safer during “close encounters with bears and lions” than with some of the armed and unfriendly people around. T he Henrichsens had apparently lived at Gumboot Lake since at least early May, when Todd Heie, another camper who visits the lake regularly, first encountered them. In early June, Joseph Charles Henrichsen, who goes by his middle name, asked a neighbor at the campground, Kevin Airoldi, for a lift into town. On the 45-minute drive, Charles said that he and his son were “just traveling around, trying to do it on the cheap.” Charles mentioned that they’d come down from the Pacific Northwest but not what he’d left behind. He’d once been a successful mortgage-loan broker in Orange County, California. But he had run into business trouble, and his relationship with Phoenix’s mother had fallen apart. By 2022, he was divorced and living near Bellingham, Washington, up by the Canadian border. That year, he spent six months in a county jail, charged with a hate crime for allegedly harassing his neighbor. Police said that he “appeared to be spiraling in his mental health,” according to court documents. Henrichsen, who kept multiple guns at his home, would rant about world events, including the war in Ukraine; an evaluation found that he likely had schizophrenia or another psychotic disorder. Although a judge ordered him to be admitted to a hospital for psychiatric treatment, bureaucratic delays kept him out for months. Even then, he was admitted only briefly, after the charges had been dropped. At Gumboot Lake, both Charles and Phoenix Henrichsen tended to keep to themselves in their Feather Ultra Lite trailer, parked amid the lodgepole pines. The other campers would watch them pacing around the lake, lap after lap, as the father appeared to loudly lecture, or preach, to the son, who kept his head down and rarely said a word. Many found Charles intense and standoffish. He would burn red sage during the day, and at night he would play a type of chanting Indian music that Heie, a former director of the county’s department of corrections, sometimes listened to as he drifted in his kayak, looking up at the sky. At one point, Aaron Sullivan, a software engineer who was working remotely out of a Winnebago along the lake, stopped by the Henrichsens’ campsite. He’d been impressed by Charles’s strong, lean frame and “big, beautiful beard.” Sullivan invited them to one of the full-moon gatherings. We won’t be doing that , Charles told him. The Thursday morning of the kidnapping, on July 16, Charles Henrichsen must have been watching the biologists before he approached them—it’s unclear how long. After he had captured the women and herded one of them into the pickup truck, he kept her tightly restrained. He told the unidentified recipient of the message he left while driving down the mountain that “her hands are behind her fucking back, and I’ve got live rounds ready to fucking [inaudible] anyone who fucks with me,” according to the criminal complaint. When Siskiyou County Sheriff Jeremiah LaRue was alerted to the situation that morning, he thought the man could be swatting, he told me—attempting to trick his office into scrambling to respond. His county is larger than Connecticut, and more than half of it is public land. Sheriff’s deputies soon arrived at Gumboot Lake to find the campsite gate closed and a gray Subaru blocking the road. (The Subaru, police would later learn, was stolen, possibly by the Henrichsens, and likely parked there to block others from entering during the kidnapping.) The sheriff’s deputies flew a drone overhead and quickly spotted the Forest Service truck that Henrichsen had commandeered, LaRue said. A man stepped out of the trailer, carrying a rifle, and later the deputies saw him with someone whose hands were bound. “He’s now pointing a rifle at the drone,” a deputy said over the radio. LaRue knew he had to get more people up there. Police set up in a dirt roundabout on the north side of the lake, within shouting distance of Henrichsen’s trailer, where he had holed back up with Phoenix and both biologists; they blocked access to the campground, and law enforcement streamed in from California and elsewhere, their cars crowding the narrow Forest Service road. Hank Magnuski, a retired tech executive who owned a nearby cabin, came upon the pileup of armored vehicles and heavily armed agents in the early afternoon, at the end of a long drive from his home in Palo Alto. He was startled by the military-style occupation of this out-of-the-way wilderness, but he gave two SWAT-team members a ride up the road. “What’s the occasion?” he asked one of them. At about 3:30 p.m, more than four hours after his initial calls, Henrichsen’s voice came over law-enforcement radio. He had taken one of the biologists back to their truck, where she helped him access the radio to contact the Forest Service’s dispatcher and the FBI. He seemed calm; he repeated his request to speak with FBI officials, “so I can release these hostages. Over.” The reception was choppy enough that he started negotiating with the FBI agent Russell Quiniola about how they might speak in person. “Are you comfortable putting the rifle down and coming to a point where you feel safe?” Quiniola asked. “Listen, you come and talk to me,” Henrichsen responded. “I would suggest coming unarmed, because if you have one, that might trigger something in me, you never know. Or you may have a rifle, and you see me, that might trigger something in you. But I suggest we get the show on the road. These ladies would like to go home. Over.” The fact that Henrichsen had initiated contact with authorities by requesting to talk with the FBI was, to some degree, encouraging. It suggested that his intentions went beyond simply harming the biologists, Gary Noesner, a former chief of the FBI’s crisis-negotiation unit, told me. In such situations, every hour that negotiators can keep the kidnapper talking is one without violence. Unless they sense that the risk is increasing, Noesner said, “we’ll talk ’til the cows come home.” Quiniola and other FBI agents spoke with Henrichsen over the next nine hours. By 1 a.m., the standoff had gone on so long with such little progress that LaRue was surprised when someone in his vehicle said, “One of the females is coming out,” and the first biologist opened the door of the trailer and walked toward the police. Her colleague followed six minutes later. Another hour and a half would pass, during which FBI agents exploded flash-bangs around the trailer—a commotion heard by hikers on the Pacific Crest Trail above the lake—before Phoenix and then Charles finally turned themselves over and the government vehicles lining the road to Gumboot Lake started heading back down the mountain. B y the time I arrived at the lake, almost all signs that this place had been the site of such force were gone. The Henrichsens’ trailer had been towed away; their debris had been bagged and left in the outhouse, along with a note that read, “Trash from the kidnappers campsite.” One camper had held on to three wooden billy clubs found amid the mess. I set up my tent at a campsite next to the Henrichsens’, where I could see the lake through the pines. Everything was serene. The day was cloudless, and the sun sparkled on the water. Charles and Phoenix Henrichsen eventually pleaded not guilty in federal court in Sacramento to charges of kidnapping federal employees and other felony counts that carry the prospect of life in prison. Charles’s lead defense attorney, Mia Crager, told me that her client had intended no harm to the biologists; according to police, the two women, who have not been named publicly, did not appear to suffer major injuries during their 15 hours as hostages. “What happened on July 16 was preventable and resulted from system failures on a number of levels,” Crager said in a statement. She did not elaborate on the type of failures she was referring to, and didn’t respond to questions about any specific allegations against Hendrichsen. She said that Charles “hopes that some good will come of the case, including that his son Phoenix will get the mental health care he sorely needs.” Phoenix’s lawyer, Kresta Daly, told me that Phoenix had been an unwilling participant in the standoff: He had no gun, didn’t know what was going to happen, and, once the crisis had started, he hoped that it would resolve peacefully. His main thought, Daly said, was “How do I stop anyone from dying today, me included?” His father, Daly told me, had hurt him before; he’d been in the hospital earlier this summer after Charles beat him up. Charles Henrichsen, through his lawyers, did not respond to questions about that accusation, but agreed that his son “was not at all at fault for what happened that day, nor was he an active participant.” Henrichsen’s specific demands during the hostage crisis have not yet been fully explained. He did not leave a manifesto. An FBI spokesperson declined to describe those hours of discussions with Henrichsen, citing the ongoing investigation. Sheriff LaRue, who had been inside a Bearcat with the FBI negotiators during part of the process, said he couldn’t hear Henrichsen “discussing anything as to why he was doing this, what his motives were.” At least in that moment, he seemed to want the attention of the federal government. He got it. The day of the biologists’ release, the chief of the Forest Service, Tom Schultz, wrote an email to agency staff expressing his gratitude to law enforcement and his support for the two women after their ordeal. A safety manager with the agency followed up the next week, with links to security tips and videos with titles such as “Avoiding Trouble” and “Building Trust in Small Towns.” Despite such internal gestures, some former Forest Service leaders heard little public support for the staff from an administration that has shed civil servants without much remorse. “There’s not an ounce of empathy for federal employees,” Vicki Christiansen, a former chief of the Forest Service during the first Trump administration and the Biden administration, told me. “Not an ounce.” As I talked with people at the lake, the hostage episode began to seem inseparable from the deepening neglect of our country’s public lands. Whatever the Henrichsens’ personal motives may have been, the erosion of day-to-day management has made ruptures in the fragile relations among strangers in the woods all the more likely. “They shouldn’t be letting someone stay here for months on end,” Heie, the former corrections officer, told me. In the early evening, I watched him paddle his kayak to the middle of the lake. Another man stood in the shallows, casting a fishing line. Through the trees, I heard a couple laughing. I kept looking around at the peaceful scene, unable to shake the unsettling feeling that something was off. As darkness settled, I sat in my camping chair, listening for the sounds of the frogs.

items.title: Mahama urges Non-Aligned Movement members to strengthen Global South influence
items.description: President John Dramani Mahama has called on members of the Non-Aligned Movement (NAM) to build on their shared interests to strengthen their collective voice and ensure the Global South has greater influence in international affairs. He made the call on Tuesday, September 1, while speaking at a high-level commemorative meeting in Belgrade, Serbia, marking the 65th anniversary of the First Conference of Heads of State or Government of Non-Aligned Countries. President Mahama said the diversity of the Non-Aligned Movement should be seen as a strength, with member states working together in areas of common interest. “Our diversity is a source of strength. By building on our shared interests, we can strengthen the collective voice of the non-aligned movement and focus our efforts where they make a meaningful difference.” He said Ghana remains committed to working with all members of the Movement to strengthen multilateralism and contribute to the establishment of a fairer international order. “Ghana remains committed to working with all members of the non-aligned movement to strengthen multilateralism, advance a fairer international order, and ensure the voice of the global South carries greater weight.” President Mahama said the Movement’s future direction should be guided by unity and a shared commitment to progress rather than alignment with either the East or the West. “As we look to the future, our direction remains clear: neither east nor west, but forward together.” He urged NAM members to draw on the spirit of Belgrade and convert their collective strength into practical action that delivers benefits for their people. “With principle, purpose, and confidence, let us renew the spirit of Belgrade and translate our collective strength into practical action for the benefits of our people.” Ghana’s participation in the commemorative meeting reflects its historic position as a founding member of the Non-Aligned Movement and its commitment to sovereign equality, non-interference, peace, multilateralism, and stronger economic cooperation among developing nations.

items.title: Missiles proches de leur date d’expiration et financements bloqués : Kaja Kallas face aux limites du «soutien indéfectible» de l’UE à l’Ukraine
items.description: Kaja Kallas a reconnu le 1er septembre, a l'ouverture de la reunion informelle des ministres de la Defense de l'UE en Irlande, que le manque de missiles intercepteurs constituait desormais le principal probleme pour la defense aerienne ukrainienne. Alors que Kiev continue de demander de nouvelles livraisons, les reserves disponibles en Europe restent limitees. Bruxelles tente donc de mobiliser les stocks encore detenus par les etats membres. Kallas a indique que certains pays disposaient de missiles dont la duree de stockage arrivait bientot a expiration et les a appeles a les transferer a l'Ukraine. « Le principal probleme de l'Ukraine, ce sont les missiles pour la defense aerienne », a-t-elle declare. Faute de reserves suffisantes au sein du bloc, l'UE cherche egalement des intercepteurs aupres de pays tiers. Kallas a toutefois reconnu que ces demarches restaient difficiles. Dans le meme temps, les capacites industrielles europeennes ne permettent pas de produire rapidement les volumes de nouveaux missiles recherches par Kiev. Les efforts se concentrent des lors sur les etats qui conservent encore des reserves. L'Espagne et la Grece sont notamment sollicitees pour ceder des missiles destines aux systemes Patriot. Athenes reste toutefois reticente a reduire ses propres stocks, qu'elle considere necessaires a sa defense. 6,6 milliards d'euros toujours bloques Les difficultes europeennes ne concernent pas seulement les munitions. Kallas a egalement indique que 6,6 milliards d'euros de la Facilite europeenne pour la paix (FEP) restaient bloques depuis 2023 en raison de desaccords entre les etats membres. Bruxelles n'est toujours pas parvenue a regler la question de la repartition de cette enveloppe. Les discussions portent notamment sur la part qui pourrait etre consacree a l'Ukraine et celle qui reviendrait aux pays de l'Union. Les ministres ont parallelement aborde la cooperation entre les industries de defense europeennes et ukrainiennes, l'utilisation du credit europeen destine a Kiev ainsi que la poursuite des livraisons militaires. Aucune decision concrete en Irlande Malgre ces discussions, aucune decision operationnelle n'etait attendue a l'issue de la reunion. « C'est une reunion informelle, nous ne prenons donc aujourd'hui aucune decision concrete », a declare Kallas. La rencontre survient ainsi alors que l'UE peine toujours a reunir les missiles demandes par Kiev, que ses capacites de production restent insuffisantes a court terme et que plusieurs milliards d'euros demeurent bloques par les divergences entre les etats membres. Moscou souligne de son cote depuis le debut du conflit que l'augmentation des livraisons occidentales d'armements a l'Ukraine ne favorise pas un reglement et contribue au contraire a prolonger les hostilites. La Russie considere egalement que les cargaisons d'armes occidentales destinees aux forces ukrainiennes constituent des cibles legitimes pour son armee.

items.title: Ekiti 2027: APC, ADC, 10 other parties set for battle over 26 Assembly seats
items.description: By Rotimi Ojomoyela, Ado-Ekiti The All Progressive Congress (APC), African Democratic Congress (ADC) and ten other political parties have fielded 174 candidates for the 26 seats in the Ekiti State House of Assembly in the 2027 general election. This was contained in a document signed and made available to journalists by the Ekiti State Legal Officer I of the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), Sina Ogundana. The document showed that the All Progressives Congress (APC), African Democratic Congress (ADC), New Nigeria Peoples Party (NNPP), National Democratic Congress (NDC) and Social Democratic Party (SDP) each fielded candidates in all the 26 constituencies. The Action Peoples Movement (APM) fielded 19 candidates, while the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) has eight candidates. The Labour Party (LP) is contesting five seats. Others on the list are the Action Alliance (AA) with four candidates, Action Democratic Party (ADP) with three, Young Progressives Party (YPP) with three and Accord, which fielded two candidates. items.title: Incendies : l’Algérie dévoile un plan en 5 points pour reconstruire les zones sinistrées
items.description: Face aux ravages causés par les incendies , l'Algérie a choisi la démarche à suivre : celle de reconstruire les zones sinistrées et d’indemniser les citoyens impactés, rapidement. C’est ce qui ressort de la réunion présidée lundi 31 août par le Premier ministre, Sifi Ghrieb. Cette réunion a eu lieu en présence des ministres concernés et a aussi connu la participation, par visioconférence, des walis. Elle entre dans le cadre de l’application des directives du président de la République, Abdelmadjid Tebboune, a souligné le Premier ministre. Un plan en cinq points a été dévoilé. La réunion a commencé par une minute de silence à la mémoire des victimes des incendies. Ensuite, le Premier ministre a détaillé les orientations et les instructions du président de la République en vue de leur « réalisation effective » dans les délais impartis, avec un calendrier précis. 1- Rétablir la totalité des réseaux avant le 5 septembre C’est donc une véritable « feuille de route » qu’a dévoilée le Premier ministre, qui a évoqué notamment une opération de rétablissement de l'approvisionnement en eau, en électricité et en télécommunications et la réouverture des routes et des sentiers dans les zones sinistrées. Pour ce faire, le Premier ministre a chargé de l’exécution de ce chantier les ministres de l’Hydraulique, de l'Énergie, de la Poste et des Télécommunications, et des Travaux publics. Il leur a fixé le samedi 5 septembre comme dernier délai. 2- Indemnisation des victimes avant le 15 septembre Le Premier ministre a ensuite abordé l’opération de recensement et d'évaluation des pertes dues aux derniers incendies, et ce, « en vue d’opérer des indemnisations avec un taux de 100 % à la charge de l’État ». L’indemnisation « englobe toutes les pertes, quelle que soit leur nature (habitations, objets égarés, cultures, arbres fruitiers, ruches, cheptels ovin, caprin et bovin ainsi que volailles », a-t-il assuré. Il a déclaré, citant le président de la République, que « le moindre objet détruit, fût-ce même un seul clou, devra être indemnisé ». Il a fixé le dernier délai pour l’achèvement de l’opération d’indemnisation au 15 septembre prochain. 3- Recenser les dégâts avant le 5 septembre Sifi Ghrieb a tenu à souligner que « l’État dispose de tous les moyens matériels, humains et logistiques » pour prendre en charge l’indemnisation de toutes les pertes causées par les incendies. Le Premier ministre a chargé le ministre de l’Intérieur, Saïd Sayoud, de clôturer l’opération de recensement avant le samedi 5 septembre, appelant au passage les walis à « privilégier l'action de terrain et de proximité avec le citoyen, et de s'éloigner de toute forme de bureaucratie, notamment lors de la reconstitution des documents et dossiers administratifs détruits », indique un communiqué de ses services. « Je ne veux aucune négligence », a-t-il dit. 4- Réparer les habitations endommagées Le Premier ministre a aussi chargé le ministre de l’Habitat, Mohamed Tarek Belaribi, de « trouver une formule contractuelle avec les entreprises de réalisation pour la réfection et la réhabilitation des habitations impactées par les incendies en vue de les délivrer à leurs propriétaires dans les délais fixés ». Les ministères de l’Habitat et des Travaux publics seront ainsi chargés d’établir une liste restreinte des entreprises qui vont être chargées de « la rénovation et la réhabilitation des habitations et les institutions impactées par les incendies, notamment les écoles et les infrastructures vitales », ajoute le Premier ministre. 5- Réformer la construction dans les zones forestières Le Premier ministre a également ordonné la mise en place d’une « étude spéciale » en vue de « préparer une loi qui porte sur les critères d’habitation dans les zones forestières afin de protéger les citoyens des dangers des incendies ». Dimanche, le président Tebboune a demandé au ministre de l’Habitat de préparer une nouvelle loi pour encadrer la construction d’habitations dans les zones forestières en fixant des normes afin de protéger les citoyens en cas d’incendies. L’article Incendies : l’Algérie dévoile un plan en 5 points pour reconstruire les zones sinistrées est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: 2027 Presidency: Court adjourns Atiku’s suit challenging Tinubu’s eligibility to Sept 28
items.description: …as judge gags parties from discussing case on social media By Ikechukwu Nnochiri, Abuja The Federal High Court sitting in Abuja on Tuesday fixed September 28 for further proceedings on the suit seeking to stop President Bola Tinubu from seeking re-election in 2027 over alleged certificate forgery. The suit, marked FHC/ABJ/CS/1888/2026, was brought before the court by a former vice president and presidential candidate of the African Democratic Congress (ADC), Atiku Abubakar. While the ADC was joined as the 2nd plaintiff, President Tinubu, his political party the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC), and the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) were listed as 1st to 3rd defendants, respectively. Specifically, Atiku, in a 25-paragraph affidavit he personally deposed to in support of the suit, alleged that President Tinubu submitted a bogus National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) discharge certificate to INEC in aid of his qualification for the presidential seat. Insisting that President Tinubu gave false information about himself in the Form CF0001 he tendered before INEC, the plaintiffs drew the court’s attention to the fact that the NYSC certificate he submitted to the electoral body bears the name “Tinubu Bola Adekunle”. “I know that the NYSC certificate is clearly not one obtained by the 1st defendant, as it belongs to one Adekunle. “The said NYSC certificate, bearing the name Tinubu Bola Adekunle, is herein attached and marked as Exhibit P2. “I know that the said NYSC certificate is still in existence and in the custody of the 3rd defendant (INEC) and that it is a forgery, as the 1st defendant’s name is not Adekunle, and yet he submitted it to the 3rd defendant to be acted upon as genuine,” Atiku averred. He told the court that Tinubu had been parading the forged certificate since 1999, when he contested the Lagos State governorship election. Atiku therefore urged the court, among others, to determine “Whether, in view of the limitations in sections 138(1)(a) & (b) of the Electoral Act, 2026, and section 285(14)(c) of the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, 1999 (As Amended), the Plaintiffs will not be allowed to enforce the binding provision of section 137(1)(j) of the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, 1999 (As Amended), which applies, mutatis mutandis, to all candidates aspiring to the office of President of the Federal Republic of Nigeria.” As well as “Whether the 1st and 2nd Defendants should be disqualified for presenting a forged NYSC certificate to the 3rd Defendant for the 2023 and 2027 Presidential Elections, in breach of Section 137(1)(j) of the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, 1999 (as amended).” Upon a positive determination of the legal questions, the plaintiffs sought a “declaration that the 1st Defendant presented a forged certificate to the 3rd Defendant when he contested for Governor of Lagos State in 1999 and thereby breached the provision of section 137(1)(j) of the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, 1999 (as amended)”. Likewise, “An order disqualifying the 1st and 2nd Defendants from participating in the 2027 Presidential Election for presenting a forged certificate to the 3rd Defendant when the 1st Defendant contested for Governor of Lagos State in 1999.” Meanwhile, when the case was called up on Tuesday, a team of lawyers led by Mr Omosanya Popoola announced their appearance for President Tinubu, whom Atiku’s lawyer, Mr Joseph Onu, said they had been unable to serve with a copy of the suit. Despite Popoola’s assurance that President Tinubu had given him the authority to represent him, Onu, however, insisted that, owing to the sensitive nature of the case, his client would prefer to effect personal service of the process or secure an order for substituted service. “My lord, this is a very important case, and we do not want to leave any chance for a technicality. We do not want to fall into any trap. “But if we have a written undertaking from the 1st defendant to be served through counsel, we will accept,” Onu insisted. For his part, INEC’s lawyer, Dr Alex Iziyon, SAN, urged the court to dismiss Atiku’s insistence on personal service of the processes on Tinubu, arguing that the appearance of his counsel was a sufficient undertaking. Noting that over 17 days had passed since the case was filed before the court, INEC demanded an expedited hearing, saying it was ready to file its defence within 10 days. After listening to all the parties, Justice Inyang Ekwo held that he could not dictate to the plaintiffs how to conduct their case. Consequently, he adjourned the matter for mention. However, the court vowed to take drastic action against any party that discussed details of the pending case in the media. “This case is to be conducted in the court and not in the media, whether it is regular or social. “If this case is discussed on social media, I will hold counsel for the party responsible, and I will take very drastic action,” Justice Ekwo warned. items.title: Burkina : Plus de 379 000 gîtes larvaires détruits lors de la première phase de la lutte antivectorielle
items.description: Burkina : Plus de 379 000 gîtes larvaires détruits lors de la première phase de la lutte antivectorielle Ouagadougou, 31 août 2026 (AIB)- Plus de 379 000 gîtes larvaires ont été détruits sur plus de 418 000 identifiés lors de la première phase des Journées nationales de lutte antivectorielle, soit un taux de destruction annoncé de 89,26 %, a indiqué lundi le ministre de la Santé, Robert Lucien Jean-Claude Kargougou, qui a salué une « mobilisation exceptionnelle » des populations. Au total, environ 418 000 gîtes larvaires ont été identifiés, dont un peu plus de 379 000 détruits, soit un taux de destruction annoncé de 89 %. Plus de 47 000 pneus usagés ont également été identifiés et collectés, tandis que plus de 188 kilomètres de canaux ont été curés. « Ces résultats ont été obtenus grâce à la forte mobilisation du gouvernement et de la population jusque dans les villages les plus reculés du pays lors de la première phase des Journées nationales de lutte antivectorielle, tenue les 8 et 9 août 2026 », a déclaré le ministre Kargougou lors d’une visioconférence consacrée au bilan de ladite phase. Pour le ministre, ces opérations contribuent à réduire la population des moustiques et, par conséquent, à lutter contre le paludisme et les autres maladies à transmission vectorielle. Malgré les résultats encourageants de cette première phase, le ministre a appelé les populations à maintenir leurs efforts, soulignant que le moustique « ne connaît pas de campagne ». « Il continue inexorablement de piquer chaque fois qu’il peut. C’est pour cela qu’il est important que nous maintenions la pression sur le moustique », a-t-il déclaré. La deuxième phase des Journées nationales de lutte antivectorielle est prévue les 5 et 6 septembre 2026. Elle devra permettre de poursuivre l’identification et la destruction des gîtes larvaires et l’assainissement des cadres de vie. À cette occasion, M. Kargougou a lancé, au nom du gouvernement, un appel à l’ensemble des Burkinabè à se mobiliser individuellement et collectivement pour que « nous puissions aller vers l’identification des gîtes larvaires, que nous puissions les détruire, et que nous puissions véritablement assainir notre cadre de vie ». Le ministre a rappelé que cette démarche s’inscrit dans la vision du président du Faso, le capitaine Ibrahim Traoré, qui a invité les Burkinabè à assainir leurs environnements de vie et de travail. VAT/ob/yos

items.title: Koosin/Education : Le nouveau CCEB de Bourasso appelle à une franche collaboration pour réussir sa mission
items.description: BURKINA-KOOSIN-EDUCATION-PASSATION-SERVICE Koosin/Education : Le nouveau CCEB de Bourasso appelle à une franche collaboration pour réussir sa mission Bourasso, 31 août 2026 (AIB)-Le gestionnaire des ressources humaines de la Koosin, Roland Guiguemdé, représentant le directeur provincial en charge de l’Enseignement de base, a installé ce lundi 31 août 2026, l'inspecteur Yelkouhan Abel Somé, dans ses nouvelles fonctions de Chef de la circonscription d'éducation de Base (CCEB) de Bourasso. La passation de charge s'est déroulée en présence des directeurs d'écoles ainsi que des autorités administratives, coutumières, religieuses et des acteurs de l'éducation de Bourasso. Le Chef de la circonscription d'éducation de Base (CCEB) entré, l'inspecteur Yelkouhan Abel Somé remplace ainsi l'inspecteur Maliki Sidibé qui a passé 09 ans à la tête de ladite CEB. Camarade Somé a remercié sa hiérarchie pour la confiance placée en lui et a félicité son prédécesseur pour les résultats engrangés. Conscient des enjeux de la mission, il a lancé un appel à tous les acteurs de l'éducation de la CEB à une franche collaboration. Le nouveau CCEB de Bourasso a également sollicité leur appui constant pour la réussite de cette mission. Le CCEB sorti, Maliki Sidibé, a remercié l'ensemble des enseignants, les acteurs de l'éducation et la population pour leur franche collaboration. Il a principalement félicité les directeurs d'écoles qui sont les pionniers pour la réouverture de la CEB de Bourasso. « Il a fallu votre sens élevé du patriotisme pour que la commune puisse bénéficier de l'éducation après quelques années de fermeture », a-t-il déclaré. Camarade Sidibé a par ailleurs demandé aux personnels de bureau, aux directeurs d'écoles, aux enseignants et à la population de soutenir le CCEB entrant pour la réussite de sa mission. Le représentant du directeur provincial, Roland Guiguemdé, a félicité l'inspecteur Maliki Sidibé pour les 09 années passées à la tête de la CEB malgré les difficultés rencontrées, avant de prodiguer des conseils au CCEB entré pour la réussite de sa mission. Une nouvelle page s'ouvre ainsi pour la CEB de Bourasso, placée sous le signe de la continuité. Agence d’information du Burkina KK/AC/HB/OO

items.title: La France surendettée : dénonçant un «casse voté au Parlement», Sarah Knafo dénonce «des milliers de coupables», des présidents successifs aux bureaucrates
items.description: « Comment est-ce que vous appelez cela ? Qu'un salarie a 2 000 euros ait donne 1 million d'euros tout au long de sa vie a l'etat francais ? » – hors TVA sur ses achats et taxes locales – a interpelle Sarah Knafo ce 1er septembre sur RTL, a l'heure ou le gouvernement planche sur de nouvelles coupes dans les depenses sociales a l'approche de l'elaboration du budget 2027. « Avec cet argent, il aurait pu s'acheter une villa au bord de la mer », a souligne l'eurodeputee et membre de Reconquete, a la veille de la parution de son livre-enquete Le Casse du siecle (ed. Fayard), depeint comme un « polar fiscal ». « Ils vous ont tout vole. Ils ont tout detruit. Et ils tiennent tout le systeme », lancait-elle sur les reseaux sociaux, en promouvant son ouvrage. « En echange de ce million d'euros, qu'est-ce qu'il va obtenir : des urgences saturees, un etat qui se fait voler ses donnees fiscales, qui n'a pas assez de canadairs pour eteindre ses feux de foret, qui n'equipe pas ses Ehpad », a-t-elle egrene face a un Marc-Olivier Fogiel prompt a vouloir lui donner la contradiction. « Vous dites qu'en gros, ceux qui nous ont gouvernes sont des assassins ? », a insiste a plusieurs reprises ce proche des Macron , lui reprochant notamment « de jouer sur la peur et la frustration des Francais » et de prendre la defense d'un « etat qui protege les Francais ». « Pire qu'un complot » « Pourquoi est-ce pire qu'un complot ? », a poursuivi Sarah Knafo, refusant l'emploi de ce terme ou de « plan secret » derriere ce « casse » chiffre en « milliers de milliards d'euros ». « Parce qu'un complot, ca se cache, la on parle d'un casse qui est vote au Parlement, qui est publie au Journal officiel, qui est promulgue par les presidents de la Republique, president apres president : il y a des milliers de coupables », a-t-elle lance en renvoyant a la mauvaise gestion chronique d'un pays dont la dette publique cumulait fin 2025 a 3 460 milliards d'euros. Interrogee sur les « perdants », autres que les « bureaucrates » de son plan de 130 milliards d'euros d'economies, via une baisse des impots et des depenses publiques, celle-ci a repondu : « Quand vous avez 150 millions d'euros qui partent en Jordanie pour la budgetisation sensible aux genres, bah oui les Jordaniens vont perdre 150 millions d'euros, quand vous avez 434 millions d'euros de l'argent des Francais qui partent pour decarboner le Costa Rica, bah oui le Costa Rica va perdre 434 millions d'euros […] mais ca ne sont pas les Francais qui vont perdre ».

items.title: 152 terrorists killed, 142 arrested, 219 surrender as Zulum hails troops
items.description: By Ndahi Marama, Maiduguri At least 152 members of Boko Haram/ISWAP terrorists have been killed, with 142 others arrested by Troops of Operation HADIN KAI (OPHK) in significant operational successes across the North East theatre between 1 and 31 August 2026. He added that a total of 219 terrorists surrendered to the security forces during the period under review. This is as Governor Babagana Umara Zulum of Borno State commended troops for their courage, resilience and sustained commitment to maintaining security across communities and creating the conditions necessary for the restoration of civilian lives. This was disclosed in an update by the Acting Media Information Officer, Headquarters Joint Task Force North East Operation HADIN KAI, Captain Mohammed Goni, in a press statement on Tuesday. He said, “From August 1st to 31st, 2026, troops neutralised 152 terrorists in ground/air operations and arrested 142 terrorists and logistics suppliers, while significantly 219 terrorists surrendered to the security forces. “The development reflects sustained pressure on terrorist networks and continued degradation of their capacity to operate across the theatre. “The operation also recorded 10 air interdictions, conducted in support of ground operations, while troops and Explosive Ordnance Disposal teams neutralised nine Improvised Explosive Devices (IEDs), denying terrorists the opportunity to employ the devices against troops and civilians.” He added: “In the course of operations, troops recovered 58 weapons and explosive items, including AK-47 rifles, an AK-49 rifle, rifle magazines, locally fabricated firearms, a hand grenade, a locally made pistol and an RPG bomb. They also recovered 1,184 rounds of ammunition. “Further recoveries included 16 mobility assets, comprising a Toyota Isuzu, four Golf wagons, six motorcycles, three bicycles and two tricycles. Troops also recovered 44 mobile phones, a Sony video camcorder and ₦1,794,910, among other items. “The August operational statistics underscore the sustained and coordinated efforts of Operation HADIN KAI across the theatre to dismantle terrorist networks, disrupt their logistics, deny freedom of action and create conditions for the restoration of lasting peace and stability in the North East.” Zulum hails Troops Meanwhile, Goni said Governor Babagana Zulum, on Monday, 31 August 2026, visited the Headquarters Joint Task Force (North East) Operation HADIN KAI (OPHK), following his working visit to 68 Battalion, Nigerian Army, Mallam-Fatori, Headquarters of Abadam Local Government Area of Borno State. During the visit, the governor commended troops of OPHK “for their courage, resilience and sustained commitment to maintaining security across the border communities and creating the conditions necessary for the restoration of civilian lives”. Governor Zulum’s engagement with the Theatre Commander, according to Goni, provided an opportunity to review the security situation in the Mallam-Fatori axis and ongoing efforts by OPHK to consolidate military gains, secure liberated communities and sustain the conditions required for the return of displaced populations. The governor acknowledged the critical role of the military in securing liberated communities and assured OPHK of the continued support of the Borno State Government, particularly in providing essential requirements to enhance troops’ operational effectiveness. The engagement further highlighted the state government’s efforts to accelerate the resettlement of more liberated communities across Borno State and facilitate the safe and dignified return of refugees from neighbouring countries. These efforts complement the security gains achieved by OPHK and are aimed at restoring essential services, rebuilding communities and creating conditions for sustainable return and reintegration. Earlier at 68 Battalion, Mallam-Fatori, Governor Zulum interacted with the Commanding Officer, Lieutenant Colonel Daniel Chiwar, senior officers and troops deployed to the area. He commended their steadfastness and commitment to securing the border community and assured them of continued government support. The Theatre Command OPHK appreciated the continued partnership and support of the Borno State Government and reaffirmed its commitment to sustaining coordinated military operations to protect communities, secure critical infrastructure and facilitate the safe return of displaced persons across the theatre.
